title: Latency amplification under batch packing: A100/H100/L40S cross-SKU study
body:
Summary:
This is an exploratory investigation into a reproducible phenomenon we started seeing on the hosted fleet: increased tail amplification when the runtime performs aggressive batch packing (multi-request within a single inference step). The goal of this doc is to capture the experiment matrix, raw observations, hypotheses for root causes, and quick mitigations to validate. Focused hardware: NVIDIA A100 (40GB/80GB variants), H100 (80GB), L40S. Cloud SKUs: gcp-a2-highgpu (A100), gcp-a3 (H100), aws-p4d/p5d, azure-nv-skus approximations. Drivers/CUDA tested: 11.8, 12.1, 12.2; NVIDIA driver builds from 510.x up through 535.x where available. Quantization modes: fp16, int8/q4, q8_0.

Why this matters:
We rely on packing to improve throughput for short requests. However, customers with strict latency SLOs are reporting intermittent p99 spikes coincident with higher packing ratios. This impacts PLG experience (signup chatbot flows) and dedicated customers with narrow latency SLAs.

Experiment design (what I ran):
- Workload: causal LLM generation (Redwood curated open model, ~7B) with variable prefix length.
- Request size: prompt tokens sampled from production percentile distribution (10/32/64).
- Concurrency driver: k6 load generator producing Poisson arrival process to mimic bursts.
- Packing window: 0ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms (our runtime batches requests arriving within window up to model max batch).
- Batching strategies: dynamic packing (pack up to N), fixed-batch (pad to N), and greedy-early (send when any request reaches length threshold).
- Measured: p50/p95/p99 latency for first-token, tail latency for end-to-end, GPU utilization, PCIe throughput, NVLink counters, memory bandwidth (nvidia-smi dmon + Nsight sampling), kernel-level contention (NVTX traces).

Matrix sample (abbreviated):
SKU | CUDA | driver | quant | pack_ms | batch_cap | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | notes
A100-80 | 11.8 | 525.85 | fp16 | 0 | 8 | 45 | 120 | 210 | baseline
A100-80 | 11.8 | 525.85 | fp16 | 25 | 32 | 60 | 220 | 480 | large p99 amplification when pack_ms>10
H100-80 | 12.2 | 535.54 | fp16 | 25 | 32 | 55 | 150 | 320 | p99 better than A100 but still amplified
L40S | 12.1 | 530.30 | q4 | 25 | 32 | 75 | 260 | 610 | quantized path increases variability
A100-80 | 12.2 | 535.54 | int8 | 10 | 16 | 58 | 200 | 440 | driver 12.2 reduces some p95 but p99 persists

Key observations (what surprised me):
- Tail amplification scales superlinearly with the effective packing ratio (requests per packed batch). At small packing windows (5–10ms) we see modest wins; beyond ~15ms pack window p99 starts rising sharply.
- H100 consistently shows lower median and p95 than A100 at large batches, but p99 is still non-trivial (suggests scheduler/tail effects outside pure FLOP throughput).
- L40S with aggressive quantization (q4/q8) increased variance — median better, tails much worse. Suspect quantization code paths interact poorly with our buffer allocation and copy patterns under concurrency.
- CUDA/driver version matters: 12.2 + driver 535.x had noticeably smoother p95 on H100 and A100 (reduced kernel launch jitter), but p99 still present. Earlier drivers (510–520) showed more frequent micro-pauses.
- NVLink vs PCIe: SKUs with NVLink (multi-GPU p2/p3d-like setups) reduced end-to-end tail when cross-GPU KV-cache transfers occurred. Single-GPU PCIe heavy traffic (large model + host->device comms) showed spikes aligned with PCIe DMA bursts.

Trace-level findings:
- NVTX traces show that the majority of p99 tails are caused by one of these: (a) a long host-side serialization waiting for a lock on a memory pool, (b) stalled DMA due to PCIe contention when multiple processes share the same NIC-PCIe root complex, (c) episodic kernel preemption when the device aborts or recovers a context (rare but visible on older drivers).
- When batch packing leads to large batch sizes, the kernel invocation graph becomes deeper (more blocks, longer GEMM ops) which increases the chance that a stray concurrent housekeeping job (metrics daemon, nv-hostengine thread) causes a 50–200ms perturbation visible at p99.

Hypotheses (root causes):
1) Host-side buffer pool contention: our allocator serializes allocations under high packing ratios, causing head-of-line blocking.
2) PCIe root-complex saturation: on some cloud SKUs the PCIe link shares fabric with NIC; bursts of network traffic (from other VMs on same host) can delay DMA and amplify tails.
3) Driver/kernel scheduling jitter: older drivers less effective at isolating long-running kernels from short ones, so when a large packed batch launches a long gemm it blocks smaller critical kernels.
4) Quantization code path branching leads to additional memcpy/format conversions that are not properly batched, causing extra CPU-side work per-request that scales with pack size.

Quick mitigations tested (short experiments):
- Soft cap on pack size: limiting batches to 12 items reduced p99 by ~30–50% at cost of 8–12% throughput. Tradeoff seems acceptable for latency-SLO customers.
- Adaptive pack-windows: if runtime detects rising p95, automatically reduce pack window. Prototype reduced p99 by 40% in noise tests.
- Preallocate per-worker pinned buffers (pool size = max batch * concurrency) to avoid lock contention: improved p50/p95 modestly and reduced frequency of long tails tied to allocator stalls.
- Pin critical runtime threads to dedicated CPUs and lower background telemetry sampling frequency — reduced host-side jitter.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Validate whether the observed PCIe-related tails correlate with noisy neighbors on shared cloud hosts. Need to reproduce on colocated VMs with synthetic NIC loads.
- Re-run on isolated bare-metal (packet provided by partner) to separate driver/GPU vs host-fabric causes.
- Profile quantization routines under concurrent requests using perf + Nsight to locate cache thrashing or memcpy hotspots.
- Test with pinned NUMA placement: ensure runtime memory allocations are NUMA-local to GPU to avoid cross-socket DMA slowdowns on multi-socket hosts.

Action items (short term):
- [Sofia] Land a soft-pack-size cap feature behind a feature flag and run a 24h canary on hosted fleet serving short prompts. (ETA: 1 week)
- [Mei] Reproduce PCIe saturation scenario with synthetic NIC traffic on the problematic GCP SKU reported by ops. (ETA: 2 weeks)
- [Ravi] Add NVTX scopes around allocator + packer code to get finer grain traces for p99 events. (ETA: 3 days)
- [Liam] Validate driver 535.x across H100/A100 on dedicated lab rigs and capture kernel preemption stats. (ETA: 1 week)

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Could be worth exploring a hybrid packing strategy: quick-path for small requests (send within 5ms) and slow-path for opportunistic packing where we compress/merge KV caches first.
- Consider adding a jitter offset to pack windows to avoid synchronized bursts across shards.
- If PCIe contention is confirmed, we may need placement constraints for latency-critical Dedicated nodes (prefer hosts with NVLink or dedicated PCIe lanes).

Appendix: short command snippets used (where applicable)
- load driver: ./benchmark_driver --model redwood-7b --concurrency 64 --arrival=poisson --pack-window-ms=25 --quant=q4
- nvprof-ish collection: ncu --target-processes all --set full --section CoreProfile --log-file ncu-pack25.log <run>

Raw notes (copy of terminal outputs, trimmed):
- A100 pack25: p99 spikes at 480ms, GPU util ~94%, PCIe bw spike coincident with p99
- H100 pack25: p99 spikes at 320ms, kernel launch lat jitter reduced under 535.x
- L40S q4 pack25: p99 > 600ms in 2/50 windows, correlated with host-side memcpy delays

If anyone wants the raw ncu traces or k6 load profiles, ping me and I will drop them in the shared drive (too heavy to keep in this doc).

-- Sofia
